newsitem.title: POLAND: OPINION - NOBE QUARTERLY FORECAST FOR POLAND.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - NOBE QUARTERLY FORECAST FOR POLAND.

text.p: NOBE Independent Centre for Economic Studies quarterly
forecast of Poland's Economic Development.*
The rapid growth of the Polish economy continued during the
first two quarters of 1997. The rapid expansion of credit,
accompanied by a swift rise in real wages and personal incomes
led to a two-digit growth rate of total domestic absorption.
The supply growth, albeit impressive, was not able to catch up
with demand. As a result, the gap between demand and supply was
continuously increasing, leading to a growing trade deficit.
Such developments are in line with our expectations and
reflect the economy's search for a new growth equilibrium with
a permanent current account deficit financed through imports of
capital. What is beginning to be be increasingly dangerous,
however, is the lack of an appropriate policy response which
would allow for the stabilisation of the current account
deficit at the level of about 4-5 percent of GDP.
The situation was additionally complicated by the
catastrophic flood in south-western Poland in July 1997. The
direct effects of the flood on GDP growth, except for a
temporary slowdown in the third quarter of 1997, are not likely
to be significant. What really worries us is that the necessary
medium-run policy actions are likely to be further postponed.
As a result, the unavoidable policy adjustment in the first
half of 1998, following general elections, will probably have
to be much stronger than we previously assumed.
Economic growth in the first half of 1997 was characterised
by three main factors.
Firstly, the dynamics of domestic absorption remained very
high, both due to the fast growth of wages, incomes and
consumer credits as well as to the continuing investment boom.
The total growth of domestic absorption exceeded 11 percent
compared to the same period a year ago.
Secondly, that rapid growth was accompanied by an even
faster increase in imports (about 20 percent). As the dynamics
of exports remained such lower, the external balance further
deteriorated.
Thirdly, inflationary pressure was continuously declining,
as the whole effect of the fast growth of demand and expansive
monetary policy contributed to the deterioration of external
balance.
The situation was further complicated by the catastrophic
flood that inundated south-western Poland in July 1997. The
flood seriously disrupted economic life in a large part of the
country. Although, for the time being, flood impact estimates
are based on arbitrarily chosen assumptions, we expect GDP
growth in the third quarter to slow down below three percent,
and for the whole of 1997 we expect growth of 5.5-6 percent.
The direct impact of the flood on real economic activity is
limited. As we projected in our previous forecast, NBP raised
basic interest rates in August. However, given the likely
additional pressure on the credit expansion connected with the
rebuilding of flood-damaged areas, the central bank's move may
prove insufficient. The government will have to face up to the
challenge of increased budgetary pressure linked to additional
flood-related spending and due to much higher costs of
servicing the public debt.
Therefore, previously announced plans to cut the 1998
fiscal deficit to below two percent of GDP do not appear
feasible, Also, any move to curb wage growth seems implausible
in 1997 in view of general elections. Altogether, serious
policy actions are not likely to take place in the second half
of 1997. It implies that unavoidable policy adjustment in the
first half of 1998 will have to take place in a more
unfavourable situation and therefore will have to be stronger
than we previously assumed.
The situation in the coming four quarters is likely to be
characterised by the following factors:
1. The trade deficit will grow rapidly. For the whole of 1997
we expect the current account deficit to reach a level of 5.5
percent of GDP (over $7 billion). Such a level can still be
financed by capital inflows, but any further growth in 1998
could become dangerous. That means that the trend towards the
rapid deterioration of the trade balance should be checked
during the first half of 1998.
2. We expect some improvement in export performance to take
place in 1998 mainly due to faster economic growth in Western
Europe despite the weak German mark. The improvement will not
be enough to restore external equilibrium in Poland, but it may
help to curb the deficit.
3. Under these circumstances, current growth rates of
investment and consumer demand are not sustainable over the
long run. Our assessment is that the growth of investment will
have to be cooled down to 11-13 percent during the first half
of 1998 and the growth of consumption to about six percent.
4. A policy package stronger than we previously assumed will
probably be inevitable to achieve these targets in the first
half of 1998. Considering fiscal policy's limited field of
manoeuvre, the major role will have to be played by monetary
policy. Domestic credit expansion will have to be restricted by
higher real interest rates, accompanied by other instruments
available to the central bank. The government, in turn, should
use all measures to curb the growth of real wages in the
economy.
As the outcome of current trends and policy changes, we expect
the growth rate of domestic absorption to slow down to some six
percent in the first half of 1998 from more than 10 percent in
1997. The growth rate of exports is not likely to exceed that
of imports before the second half of 1998. The growth rate may
start picking up only after the trend of the current account
deterioration is checked (Table 1).
Table 2 shows projected inflationary developments over the next
four quarters. Inflationary pressure will still continue to
decline. However, higher inflationary expectations, and a
continuous crawling peg setting a floor for domestic inflation
will slow down the decline. The 1997 inflation target of 13
percent will probably be exceeded mainly because of the effects
of the flood. Reaching one-digit inflation in 1998, while
possible, will be extremely difficult.
The growth of industrial prices will stabilise round 11
percent. The drop in industrial prices will not resume before
the second half of 1998 after the effective crawling-peg
devaluation of the zloty is slowed down well below one percent
a month.
